quotes.verbatim_quote: These are examples of chordal movements using the six categories of chord sounds found in the <irst part of this book.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This sentence frames the entire chapter as applied harmony, tying the chord-form vocabulary from Chapter 1 to real movement contexts.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
MAJOR SOUNDS: The first four chords illustrate movement in “C”. The fifth chord is G13b5 (or Db7+9b5) which re-
solves into Cma9.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the functional logic of the major-sound passage — dominant substitution (tritone sub Db7) resolving to tonic Cma9 — establishing a core jazz cadence pattern.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
MINOR SEVENTH TO SEVENTH SOUNDS: First four chords illustrate movement in Dm7, resolving into Abl13 to
G13.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes the ii–V movement with a chromatic approach chord (Ab13), a foundational jazz harmonic device the student must internalize.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
SEVENTHS: The first three chords illustrate movement around G7. The next four chords illustrate a substitute turn-
around back to G13, followed by a cycle seventh movement.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Introduces the concept of substitute turnarounds and cycle-of-fifths seventh movement as distinct techniques within a single dominant-chord passage.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
DIMINISHED SOUNDS: Resolve the last chord in this sequence into any chord. For example: (1) Dm7 — G7 — Cma’7,
or (2) Em7 — Eb9 — Dm9 — Db9.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Gives a concrete rule — diminished chords are interchangeable approach chords — and offers two specific resolution paths that demonstrate chromatic bass-line motion.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
DIMINISHED PASSAGE: Use of diminished chords for seventh flat ninth chord movement, utilizing the basic pattern
of A7 — Dm — G7 —C.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the defining rule that a diminished chord can stand in for a 7b9 chord, anchoring the diminished passage to a recognizable I–VI–II–V skeleton.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
AUGMENTED SOUNDS: The first six chords are basically G aug. Movement is used chromatically to get to the basic
cycle (A7 — D7 —G).
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the compositional logic of the augmented passage — sustained augmented color resolved via chromatic voice-leading into a cycle cadence.

quotes.verbatim_quote: These chord symbols are written so that the order of appearance of notes coincides with the spelling of the chord symbol. For example, D7+9+5 means D7 with the raised 9th next, and the raised 5th on top.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes the book's proprietary notation rule — symbol order equals voice order — which is essential for correctly reading every voicing in the substitution tables.

quotes.verbatim_quote: NOTE: Try to sustain lead notes from one chord to the next. For example, C9 to F13, sustain the G on top.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Gives a direct performance technique — common-tone sustain across chord changes — that shapes idiomatic jazz comping and voice-leading on the guitar.

quotes.topic: Minor Seventh Flat Fifth to Seventh passage
quotes.verbatim_quote: MINOR SEVENTH FLAT FIFTH TO SEVENTH SOUNDS: A7b9 to Dm7}5 resolving finally to G aug.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Demonstrates the iiø–V7b9 half-diminished motion, a characteristic minor-key cadence the student needs to recognize and execute.

quotes.topic: Minor Seventh Flat Fifth to Augmented
quotes.verbatim_quote:
MINOR SEVENTH FLAT FIFTH TO AUGMENTED SOUNDS: Dm7b5 chords to G aug. Notice the chords used to
obtain these sounds.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Directs the student's analytical attention to the specific voicings used, flagging that the chord shapes themselves (not just the symbols) carry the lesson.
